chapter_title: Route 53 for DNS-based Failover and Routing

screens.title: Route 53 for DNS-based Failover and Routing
screens.subtitle: Use Route 53 health checks and routing policies to build resilient, multi-region DNS failover.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how Route 53 goes beyond simple name resolution to enable automated, DNS-level failover and intelligent traffic distribution. We'll look at how health checks let Route 53 detect a failing endpoint, how failover record sets redirect users to a standby region, and how routing policies like latency and weighted distribution help meet performance and testing goals. You'll also learn why DNS caching and TTL settings directly affect how quickly a failover actually reaches users in the real world. A concrete example we'll revisit is an application fronted by two Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. You will see how a health check on the primary ALB triggers Route 53 to serve the secondary ALB when the primary becomes unhealthy, and why TTL and health check intervals determine the user-visible recovery time. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to plan health checks, choose a routing policy, and make pragmatic TTL decisions that balance rapid failover with DNS query load. Think: how quickly must your users recover, and what trade-offs are you willing to accept?

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Route 53 health checks plus failover routing provide automated disaster recovery at the DNS layer, but their effectiveness depends on correct probes and realistic TTL settings.

Route 53 for DNS-based Failover and Routing

Master the health checks and routing policies that let Route 53 detect failures and route users to healthy regions. Learn practical trade-offs like TTL, check intervals, and realistic probes that confirm application health — not just server liveness.

In this lesson
Health checks, failover, routing policies
Primary health
Monitor ALBs or endpoints with application-level probes.
Automatic failover
Route 53 switches to the secondary when primary is unhealthy.
TTL trade-off
Lower TTL shortens failover visibility at the cost of more DNS queries.
Explore Key Topics
Health Checks
Probe app endpoints with HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP to determine true availability.
Failover Routing
Define primary and secondary record sets; Route 53 swaps traffic based on health.
TTL & Propagation

Coming up
A hands-on failover activity: create health checks, configure primary and secondary records, test failover, and observe TTL effects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure Route 53 health checks to monitor real application endpoints, implement failover routing records to redirect traffic automatically during outages, choose and use other routing policies like latency, weighted, and geolocation to optimize user experience, and reason about DNS caching and TTL so you know how fast failover will reach users. For each skill you'll see why it matters: health checks are the trigger that tells Route 53 when to change answers; failover records let you build an automated recovery path between regions; routing policies let you influence user placement for performance or testing; and TTL controls how long client resolvers keep old answers, directly affecting your recovery time objective. A concrete use case we will revisit is an app with ALBs in us-east-1 and us-west-2: you'll create a health check for the primary ALB, configure a primary and a secondary record, and change TTL to observe propagation. Keep in mind a common pitfall: testing only server reachability without an app-level probe can falsely report healthy status. Verify the application end-to-end to avoid that mistake.

keyIdea.title: Core aim
keyIdea.text: Turn DNS into an automated part of your disaster recovery plan by combining health checks, routing policies, and pragmatic TTL choices.

Second, you'll create failover record sets in a hosted zone: a primary record associated with the health check and a secondary record that becomes active when the primary is unhealthy. screens.title: What is Amazon Route 53?
screens.subtitle: A DNS service that supports health checks and advanced routing

narration.text: Amazon Route 53 is a highly available, scalable cloud DNS service that does more than map names to addresses. In practice for a SysOps Administrator, Route 53 becomes part of your availability strategy because it can run health checks and change DNS answers automatically. A health check can use HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP to probe an endpoint; based on the results Route 53 can consider an endpoint healthy or unhealthy and adjust which IP addresses or AWS resources it returns to clients. For example, if you host an application behind an ALB in us-east-1 and a standby ALB in us-west-2, Route 53 can be configured so that DNS queries for app. example. com resolve to the primary ALB while healthy and resolve to the secondary only if the primary's health check fails. A common misconception is to treat DNS as a passive directory; instead, Route 53 can actively influence traffic routing. The takeaway is that Route 53 combines directory service and simple automation: design health checks and records intentionally so DNS becomes a dependable recovery mechanism rather than an accidental single point of confusion.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Route 53 is DNS plus active health checking and routing policies that can automate failover and optimize traffic.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is Amazon Route 53?

Route 53 is a DNS web service that couples resolution with health checks and advanced routing policies so DNS can be used for high availability and disaster recovery.

Key behaviors
  • Responds to DNS queries for your hosted zones.
  • Performs health checks and marks endpoints healthy or unhealthy.
  • Supports routing policies that change answers based on health or rules.
Concrete example
app.example.com maps to an ALB in us-east-1 while healthy, and to an ALB in us-west-2 when the primary fails.
Common misconception
DNS is not passive here; Route 53 actively changes answers based on health checks and configured policies.
Key Takeaway

Think of Route 53 as DNS with a heartbeat: health checks are the heartbeat that drives routing decisions.

Visual: role of health checks in DNS
Probe types
HTTP, HTTPS, TCP probes confirm endpoint behavior.
Health state
Route 53 marks endpoints healthy/unhealthy and uses that state in routing policies.
Routing action
If primary is unhealthy, Route 53 returns the secondary record as the answer.

screens.title: How Route 53 Health Checks Work
screens.subtitle: Probe endpoints and update DNS answers based on health

narration.text: A Route 53 health check periodically probes an endpoint and records success or failure. The check can use HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP; importantly, you should probe an application-specific path so the check validates the service, not merely the network stack. Route 53 sends requests at configured intervals and counts failed checks before declaring an endpoint unhealthy. For example, if you set a fast interval of 10 seconds and require two consecutive failures, a genuine outage will be detected quickly. The health check result becomes an input for routing policies: failover, weighted, or latency routing can use it to include or exclude endpoints from answers. A common mistake is choosing a shallow probe such as checking the root TCP port — this can report healthy while the application itself is failing. Another misconception is that a health check alone reduces client caching delays; it does not. Health checks change Route 53’s internal view immediately, but clients will still follow cached DNS answers until TTL expires. Design checks to hit application behavior that matters, keep intervals and failure thresholds aligned to your desired recovery time objective, and always test by simulating failures and watching health check status change.

keyIdea.title: Health check mechanics
keyIdea.text: Health checks probe an endpoint repeatedly; their results determine which records Route 53 returns to clients.

content.html:
Definition

How Route 53 Health Checks Work

Health checks periodically probe endpoints. Their pass/fail state is used by routing policies to include or exclude endpoints from DNS answers.

Probe types
HTTP, HTTPS, TCP. Prefer an application-specific path that confirms functional behavior.
Intervals & thresholds
Fast intervals detect outages faster but increase checks. Use realistic failure counts that reflect your RTO.
Pitfall
Checking only TCP or the server port can falsely indicate healthy when the app is degraded.
Process flow
1
Probe endpoint
Route 53 sends HTTP/HTTPS/TCP checks at the chosen interval.
2
Evaluate responses
Count consecutive failures or successes to change health state.
3
Update routing state
Route 53 marks endpoints healthy/unhealthy and affects which records are returned.
4
Clients continue per TTL
Clients will only see the new answer once their cached TTL expires or they requery.
Key Takeaway

Design health checks to validate real application behavior; health status drives DNS answers, but TTL controls client visibility.

screens.title: Designing Effective Health Checks
screens.subtitle: Probe application functionality, set intervals, and choose thresholds

narration.text: Effective health checks are central to DNS-based failover. The most important design principle is to probe application behavior, not just server liveness. That means choosing an HTTP or HTTPS path that returns success only when the application is serving requests correctly — for example an index or a dedicated /health endpoint that verifies database or service dependencies. Use fast intervals like 10 seconds when you need rapid detection, but remember that more frequent checks increase the number of probes and can add cost. Also set sensible failure thresholds so transient errors don't trigger failover too quickly; two or three consecutive failures is common with fast intervals. Another practical tip is to monitor and alert on health check trends, not just state changes, so you see degrading performance before full failure. A frequent misconception is thinking health checks alone will make client failover instant; health checks change Route 53's internal state quickly, but clients still obey TTL. Always test your health check behavior by inducing failures and verifying both the health status and the actual DNS resolution from a client perspective. The takeaway: craft probes that reflect the user experience and align intervals and thresholds to your recovery goals.

keyIdea.title: Design focus
keyIdea.text: Probe what matters to users, tune intervals and thresholds, and test to confirm detection and recovery behavior.

content.html:
Best Practice

Designing Effective Health Checks

Make health checks validate the application experience, tune intervals, and avoid overreacting to brief glitches.

Probe an app endpoint
Use /index.html or a dedicated /health that checks service dependencies.
Choose interval & failures
Fast interval for rapid detection, and 2–3 failures to avoid reacting to transient errors.
Cost vs speed
More frequent checks increase probe traffic; balance detection speed with load.
Check design checklist
  • Use application-level paths that verify critical dependencies.
  • Prefer HTTPS for secure probes where appropriate.
  • Align intervals and failure counts to your desired RTO.
  • Monitor check trends and alert before total failure.
Key Takeaway

Health checks should reflect the end-user experience; tune them, test them, and watch for degrading trends.

screens.title: Failover Routing Policy Mechanics
screens.subtitle: Primary and secondary record sets with health checks drive automatic failover

narration.text: Failover routing uses two record sets for the same DNS name: a primary and a secondary. The primary record is associated with a Route 53 health check. While the primary is healthy, Route 53 returns its value to clients. If the health check fails, Route 53 begins returning the secondary record instead. One practical detail is the use of SetIdentifier and Weight parameters in record sets: in the conceptual CLI example you may see Weight set to 100 for primary and 0 for secondary to indicate standby behavior. The weight value interacts with certain routing types; for pure failover use the dedicated failover routing policy and mark failover record types as Primary and Secondary. When the primary recovers, Route 53 can automatically route traffic back to it. A common error is creating two simple A records without health checks — that will not provide automatic failover because Route 53 will distribute traffic without evaluating health. The correct pattern is clear: attach a health check to the primary record in a failover policy, configure TTL appropriately for your RTO, and optionally monitor the secondary with its own health check. Always test the sequence: fail primary, observe health change, and confirm DNS resolution moves to the secondary.

keyIdea.title: Failover rule
keyIdea.text: Primary record plus health check; secondary record serves when primary is unhealthy. Do not rely on simple records for failover.

content.html:
Process Flow

Failover Routing Policy Mechanics

Use primary and secondary record sets tied to health checks so Route 53 automatically redirects traffic when the primary fails.

Primary record
Attach a health check and mark as Primary within a failover routing policy.
Secondary record
Marked as Secondary; it becomes the response when primary is unhealthy.
Common mistake
Two simple records without health-checking will not provide intelligent failover.
Configuration callout
Essential fields: Name, Type (A or alias), Routing policy: Failover, Failover record type: Primary or Secondary, Set Identifier, HealthCheckId attached to primary, TTL set appropriately.
Example pattern
Primary: app.example.com → us-east-1 ALB, HealthCheckId: PrimaryALBHealthCheck. Secondary: app.example.com → us-west-2 ALB, no primary health check required for basic failover.
Testing steps
  1. Confirm primary resolves while healthy.
  2. Simulate failure and watch health check go unhealthy.
  3. Verify DNS resolves to secondary after TTL/propagation.
Key Takeaway

Use failover record sets with health checks — do not rely on simple records for automated disaster recovery.

screens.title: CLI Example: Creating Failover Record Sets
screens.subtitle: A conceptual AWS CLI example for primary and secondary records

narration.text: We'll walk through the conceptual CLI example that creates a primary and a secondary record set. The primary resource record set includes a SetIdentifier, a nonzero weight, a Region, and a HealthCheckId. This ties that record to a health check so Route 53 knows whether to serve it. The secondary resource record set is created with a weight of zero in this conceptual example to indicate standby behavior. In practice, for failover you should use the built-in failover routing policy and mark records as Primary and Secondary, attaching a health check to the primary. When you run the change-resource-record-sets command with a change batch, Route 53 stores the new records in the hosted zone and begins using them in response to queries. A frequent misunderstanding is reading weight alone as a failover switch; weight is for distributing traffic across multiple records. For deterministic failover, set routing policy to Failover and rely on the health check evaluation. After applying the commands, test by checking Route 53 health check status, performing dig or nslookup on the name, and simulating an outage to watch the DNS answer switch.

keyIdea.title: CLI pattern
keyIdea.text: Attach HealthCheckId to the primary record in a failover routing policy; use change-resource-record-sets to create records.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

CLI Example: Creating Failover Record Sets

Below is the conceptual CLI snippet from the chapter. It shows creating a primary record set with a HealthCheckId and a secondary record set intended as standby.

# Create a primary record set
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets \
    --hosted-zone-id Zxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
    --change-batch '{
        "Changes": [
            {
                "Action": "CREATE",
                "ResourceRecordSet": {
                    "Name": "app.example.com.",
                    "Type": "A",
                    "SetIdentifier": "Primary",
                    "Weight": 100,
                    "Region": "us-east-1",
                    "HealthCheckId": "hc-0abcdef1234567890",
                    "ResourceRecords": [
                        {"Value": "alb-primary-us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com"}
                    ]
                }
            }
        ]
    }'

# Create a secondary (failover) record set
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets \
    --hosted-zone-id Zxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
    --change-batch '{
        "Changes": [
            {
                "Action": "CREATE",
                "ResourceRecordSet": {
                    "Name": "app.example.com.",
                    "Type": "A",
                    "SetIdentifier": "Secondary",
                    "Weight": 0,
                    "Region": "us-west-2",
                    "HealthCheckId": "hc-0fedcba9876543210",
                    "ResourceRecords": [
                        {"Value": "alb-secondary-us-west-2.elb.amazonaws.com"}
                    ]
                }
            }
        ]
    }'
Annotations
  • HealthCheckId: ties the primary record to a check so Route 53 can evaluate health.
  • SetIdentifier: a unique label for the record set version.
  • Weight: used for traffic distribution, not the primary mechanism for failover.
  • Region: indicates the AWS region of the resource; useful for latency and management.
Key Takeaway

Use failover routing and attach a HealthCheckId to the primary record; weight is for distribution, not failover control.

screens.title: Activity: Configure Route 53 Failover for Two ALBs
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step instructions to create health checks and failover records

narration.text: This activity walks through configuring Route 53 failover for two ALBs in different regions. Start by creating a hosted zone for your domain if you don't already have one. Next create a health check named PrimaryALBHealthCheck pointing to the us-east-1 ALB using HTTP and an application health path such as /index. html; set a fast interval when you need quick detection. Then create a Primary record: record name app, type A, alias to Application Load Balancer, region us-east-1, routing policy Failover, failover type Primary, and associate the health check. Create a Secondary record with the same name, alias to the us-west-2 ALB, routing policy Failover, failover type Secondary, and TTL 60 seconds. Test failover by accessing app. yourdomain and confirming it resolves to the primary. Simulate a failure by stopping instances behind the primary or deregistering targets. Observe the health check transition, then retry resolution after the TTL to confirm it resolves to the secondary. Restore the primary and verify automatic failback. Common errors include forgetting to attach the health check or using a high TTL that slows client recovery. The exercise confirms that configuration and TTL together determine your visible recovery time.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Create health check, primary and secondary failover records, test by simulating primary outage, and observe DNS failover considering TTL.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Configure Route 53 Failover for Two ALBs

Step-by-step
  1. Create a hosted zone for your domain if needed.
  2. Create PrimaryALBHealthCheck: protocol HTTP, domain = primary ALB DNS, path = /index.html, fast interval for quicker detection.
  3. Create Primary record: name app, type A, alias to ALB in us-east-1, routing policy = Failover, record type = Primary, associate the health check, TTL = 60.
  4. Create Secondary record: same name app, type A, alias to ALB in us-west-2, routing policy = Failover, record type = Secondary, TTL = 60.
  5. Test: resolve app.yourdomain, simulate primary failure, watch health check become unhealthy, and re-resolve after TTL to confirm secondary answers.
Checks & pitfalls
  • Ensure the health check path returns success only when the app is healthy.
  • Avoid very high TTLs when you need fast failover.
  • Optionally create a health check for the secondary to detect its problems too.
Key Takeaway

Follow the lab steps exactly, then simulate failure to confirm both the health check and TTL behave as expected.

screens.title: Routing Policies: Latency, Weighted, Geolocation, Geoproximity
screens.subtitle: When to use each policy to optimize traffic

narration.text: Route 53 provides several routing policies beyond failover, each serving different operational needs. Latency-based routing sends users to the region with the lowest measured network latency, improving perceived performance for geographically dispersed users. Weighted routing lets you split traffic according to percentages you define, which is ideal for A/B testing or gradual rollouts. Geolocation routing answers queries based on the geographic origin of the DNS request, which helps serve localized content or meet residency requirements. Geoproximity routing lets you bias traffic toward or away from particular resources depending on geographic distance and an optional bias value. Each of these policies has different operational consequences: latency routing requires multiple healthy endpoints in regions to be beneficial, weighted routing must be used carefully with health checks so you don't send traffic to unhealthy endpoints, and geolocation/geoproximity routing can complicate behavior because DNS resolvers may make location-based decisions differently. A common misunderstanding is assuming routing policies bypass health checks — they do not. Combine routing policies with health checks so Route 53 excludes unhealthy resources from answers. Choose the policy that matches your objective: performance, gradual rollout, or geographic control.

keyIdea.title: Policy selection
keyIdea.text: Pick latency for performance, weighted for traffic splits, and geolocation/geoproximity for geographic control; always pair with health checks.

content.html:
Comparison

Routing Policies Overview

Choose the routing policy that aligns with your goals: lower latency, traffic experiments, or geographic targeting.

Latency-based routing
Routes users to the region with lowest measured latency for them.
Weighted routing
Distributes traffic by percentage; useful for A/B testing or blue/green deployments.
Geolocation & Geoproximity
Serve users based on query location or distance bias; useful for localization and residency.
When to pair with health checks
Always combine routing policies with health checks so Route 53 excludes unhealthy resources. For example, a weighted rollout should not send test traffic to an endpoint that is down. Similarly, latency routing is useful only when healthy endpoints exist in multiple regions.
Practical tip
Use weighted routing for gradual traffic shifts, and monitor health checks closely during rollouts.
Key Takeaway

Match policy to goal and always combine with health checks to ensure unhealthy endpoints are not returned.

screens.title: Latency vs Weighted vs Geolocation Routing
screens.subtitle: Operational differences, use cases, and common pitfalls

narration.text: To choose among latency, weighted, and geolocation routing, consider the goal: latency routing prioritizes lowest network delay, weighted routing allocates percentages for controlled rollouts, and geolocation routing answers based on where the DNS query originated. Latency routing works well when you have healthy endpoints in multiple regions and want the best response time for users. Weighted routing is the right tool for testing new versions by sending a small portion of traffic to them before full rollout. Geolocation routing helps when content or compliance depends on user location. Operational pitfalls include relying on weight without health checks, which can route traffic to unhealthy endpoints, and assuming geolocation decisions map perfectly to a user's actual experience — DNS resolvers may sit in different places than the user. Also remember that latency routing's benefit depends on accurate regional performance; if a region is unhealthy it should be removed via health checks. In practice you may combine policies: use latency routing for general performance and weighted routing for controlled experiments on a subset of traffic, always with health checks in place. The closing question to consider is which policy best supports your recovery and performance objectives while remaining testable in a disaster scenario.

keyIdea.title: Policy trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Latency focuses on performance, weighted on controlled distribution, and geolocation on locality; all must be used with health checks and testing.

content.html:
Deep Dive

Latency vs Weighted vs Geolocation Routing

Compare operational trade-offs and plan tests so the routing policy behaves during outages and rollouts.

Latency
Best for directing users to the lowest-latency region; requires healthy endpoints in each region.
Weighted
Use percentages for A/B tests or blue/green; monitor health checks during rollouts.
Geolocation
Serve content by the query origin; useful for localization and residency rules.
Common pitfalls & tests
  • Don't use weight without health checks; unhealthy endpoints can still receive traffic.
  • Test geolocation behavior from different resolvers to confirm routing.
  • Measure latency improvements before assuming user experience will significantly change.
Key Takeaway

Match the routing policy to the outcome you need, and validate with health checks and real tests from user locations.

screens.title: DNS Caching and TTL: Impact on Failover Speed
screens.subtitle: Why TTL determines the real-world recovery time of DNS-based failover

narration.text: DNS caching and the Time To Live (TTL) of a record are the keys to how quickly clients observe a failover. When a client resolver receives an IP for a name it caches that answer for the TTL period. If your record has a TTL of 24 hours, clients may continue using the cached, now-unhealthy address for up to that long even after Route 53 changes its answer. For failover scenarios we typically recommend much lower TTLs — examples in the chapter suggest 60 seconds or even 30 seconds — so clients re-resolve quickly. The trade-off is higher DNS query volume and potentially more load on your resolvers or Route 53. Another important nuance is that not all resolvers respect TTLs identically; some intermediate resolvers can impose their own caching behavior, so testing in your user path is essential. A common mistake is lowering TTL in production without measuring DNS query impact; plan for the increased queries and monitor costs and resolver behavior. In practice, pick a TTL that aligns with your recovery time objective and test failover by simulating outages while observing both health check behavior and actual client resolutions. The final question to consider is how fast users need to recover compared to the cost of additional DNS traffic.

keyIdea.title: TTL trade-off
keyIdea.text: Lower TTLs speed visible failover but increase DNS query volume; choose a TTL that matches your RTO and test it.

content.html:
Critical Consideration

DNS Caching and TTL

TTL controls how long resolvers cache DNS answers. Lower TTLs make failover visible faster but increase DNS traffic.

Effect on RTO
TTL is a primary limiter of how quickly clients see a new DNS answer after failover.
Recommended values
For failover testing use lower TTLs like 60 or 30 seconds; balance against increased query volume.
Resolver behavior
Resolvers and intermediary caches can affect propagation. Always test along the user path.
Practical test actions
  • Set TTL to 60 seconds and observe behavior during a simulated outage.
  • Use dig or nslookup from different resolvers to measure propagation.
  • Monitor Route 53 query volume and costs if you lower TTL globally.
Key Takeaway

TTL is the gate between Route 53's routing decisions and what clients actually do. Choose TTL with your RTO and resolver behavior in mind.

screens.title: Common Mistakes, Testing, and Assessment
screens.subtitle: Misconfigurations to avoid and how to validate your failover setup

narration.text: Common mistakes when implementing Route 53 failover include misconfigured health checks, overly high TTLs, and misunderstanding routing policy behavior. For instance, a health check that targets the wrong port or path will not reflect real application health; this can cause Route 53 to leave a failing app in the DNS answers. High TTLs such as 24 hours delay client adoption of a new DNS answer, making your RTO much larger than Route 53's internal failover action. Another mistake is creating two simple records and assuming Route 53 will fail over; without health checks and the failover routing policy, Route 53 simply distributes queries. To validate your configuration, follow the lab steps: create health checks, attach them to primary records, set TTL to a low test value, and simulate a primary outage by stopping instances or deregistering targets. Observe the Route 53 health check status change, then use dig or nslookup to confirm the name resolves to the secondary after the TTL expires. The assessment in the chapter reinforces this: when users are not redirected promptly, the most likely cause is a too-high TTL. Always close testing by restoring services and confirming automatic failback.

keyIdea.title: Validation focus
keyIdea.text: Test by simulating outages and observing both health check state and client DNS resolution; watch TTL effects carefully.

content.html:
Troubleshooting

Common Mistakes, Testing, and Assessment

Avoid misconfigured checks and high TTLs. Test failover by simulating outages and verifying both health checks and client resolution.

Frequent errors
Wrong health check path, high TTL, and using simple routing without health checks.
Validation steps
Simulate failure, watch health check state, use dig/nslookup to confirm the DNS answer changes after TTL.
Assessment idea
If failover takes minutes, the most likely cause is a high TTL. Lower TTL to reduce propagation time.
Check your understanding
Question: After primary becomes unhealthy, users are not redirected quickly. Which setting is most likely causing the delay? Answer: TTL is too high. This demonstrates the interaction between Route 53's internal state and resolver caching.
Key Takeaway

Validation requires both service-level failure simulation and client-side DNS checks; TTL often dictates real-world recovery time.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Remember these core ideas: Route 53 is a DNS service that can actively monitor endpoints with health checks and change DNS answers based on those results. Route 53 health checks should target application-level endpoints so they reflect real service health rather than mere server reachability. Failover routing pairs a primary record with a health check and a secondary record that receives traffic when the primary is unhealthy; do not rely on simple records for intelligent failover. These three ideas form the operational foundation of DNS-based disaster recovery. Keep them in mind as you design health checks, choose routing policies, and set TTL values that match your recovery goals.
